1.goal: To open on what she does now when she does not understand something in a meeting, and to tell her what the lesson ends with.
1.interaction: T–S, spoken. One open question; Portuguese is fine for a word she does not have.
run: Ask whether she opened the pre-class, and whether she listened to the voice message.
Tell her what the lesson ends with, in one sentence: she follows part of a meeting and asks questions when something is not clear.
Ask the question on screen and take one answer.
exact: What today is: “Today you listen to the management meeting about the laptops. Then you ask questions when something is not clear.”
If she answers in general terms: “Think of the last time. What did you do?”
1.expected: What she really does, in a few words. Answers at this level may be “I ask again” or “I wait and ask a colleague later”, and both are useful information. A complete answer names one thing she does and, if possible, one situation where it happened.
1.support: If she has no answer, offer two options: she asks at the moment, or she waits until after the meeting.
1.challenge: Ask what happened the last time she did not ask.
1.monitoring: Whether she already has a strategy, and whether she uses English or Portuguese to describe it.
1.evidence: What she says she does now when she does not understand. It is the starting point for this lesson.
1.transition: Move on when she has given one answer.

2.goal: To place the meeting in the story of lesson 1 and bring back what she already knows about the laptops.
2.interaction: T–S, reading the brief on screen together.
run: Read the situation and the brief with her.
Ask the question on screen. Accept what she remembers, in any order.
2.expected: From Ryan's email in lesson 1: the laptops did not arrive last Friday, the delivery was moved to next Thursday, the sales team has training on Tuesday, and the two options were moving the training or using the old laptops. If she did not have lesson 1, read the brief and tell her in one sentence: the new laptops are late, and the training is soon.
2.support: If she does not remember, ask one question at a time: “When was the training?” and “What were the two options?”
2.challenge: Ask which option she thinks Paula will choose, and why.
2.monitoring: Which details she remembers from lesson 1 without help.
2.evidence: What she remembers from the email, and in what words.
2.transition: Move on when the situation is clear.

3.goal: To have her make three guesses before she listens, so the first listening has something to confirm.
3.interaction: T–S, guessing out loud. The guesses stay open until the first listening.
run: Read the three questions with her.
Take one answer for each, and write them where she can see them.
Leave them unconfirmed: the audio on the next screen settles the first two.
exact: Before moving on: “These are your guesses. Now we listen and check.”
3.expected: There is no answer key on this screen. For your reference, the meeting shows that the delivery changes to Wednesday, one day earlier, and that Paula keeps the training on Tuesday with the old laptops. The third question has no fixed answer.
3.support: If she does not guess, offer two options for the second question: move the training, or keep it.
3.challenge: Ask which of her guesses she is most sure about.
3.evidence: Her guesses, kept for screen 4, and the question she would ask Ryan.
3.transition: Move on when the three questions have an answer.

4.goal: To understand the main news and the decision from one listening at normal speed, without the transcript.
run: Read the two questions on screen with her before you press Play.
Play once at Normal. The transcript stays closed on this screen.
Take her answers, then go back to her guesses from screen 3.
exact: Before pressing Play: “Listen once, all the way. Find two things: is the news good or bad, and what does Paula decide?”
4.expected: Question 1: the news is good, because the laptops now arrive one day earlier, on Wednesday. An answer like “Good. They arrive earlier.” is complete. Question 2: Paula keeps the training on Tuesday, with the old laptops, and the team gets the new laptops on Thursday.
4.support: If she caught little, play it once more at Slower and ask only the second question.
4.challenge: Ask who is going to tell the trainer.
4.monitoring: Whether she gets the decision, or only single words.
4.evidence: How much she understood from one listening at normal speed. It is the first listening measure of the cycle.
4.transition: Move on when both questions have an answer.

5.goal: To listen for details with a new purpose, and to check the answers against the transcript after the activity.
5.interaction: S listens and says her answers, you mark them on screen, then T–S to check.
run: Read the six sentences with her before you press Play, so she knows what to listen for.
Play once at Normal. She says which sentences are true and you mark them on screen; play once more at Slower if she asks.
Press Check when three are marked. Then open the transcript and find the line for each sentence together.
exact: Before pressing Play: “Read the six sentences. Now listen, and mark the three that are true.”
5.expected: True: “The delivery is now one day earlier.” (Wednesday, not Thursday) · “Someone needs to install the new system.” (“We need to install it.”) · “Ryan is going to write to the trainer.” (“I'll email her today.”). False: “The laptops arrive on Wednesday morning.” — in the afternoon, after four · “The training moves to the following week.” — it stays on Tuesday · “Installing the system takes all day.” — about two hours.
5.support: If she marks a false sentence, play the part with that detail at Slower before you open the transcript.
5.challenge: Ask when Nora is going to install the system, and why then.
5.monitoring: Which details she catches: days, times or numbers. Note the kind of information she misses.
5.evidence: Which false sentences she marked, and whether the slower speed changed her answer.
5.transition: Move on when the six are checked against the transcript.

6.goal: To have her notice that questions for unclear information do three different jobs, before the jobs are explained.
6.interaction: S says her answers and you mark them on screen, then T–S to check.
run: For each of the six questions, she says the answer and you choose it on screen. Then press Check.
Go through them out loud. On each one, ask what the speaker already knows and what they still need.
Leave the explanation for the next screen: here she only sorts.
6.expected: To hear it again: “Sorry, could you say that again?” · “Sorry, I didn't catch that.” To check one detail: “Sorry, did you say Wednesday?” · “Just to check, do the laptops come with the new system?” To confirm what they understood: “So the laptops can be ready on Thursday morning, right?” · “So we keep the training on Tuesday, right?” The two questions that people mix up are “Sorry, did you say Wednesday?” and “Sorry, could you say that again?”: in the first, the speaker heard something.
6.support: On each question, ask: did this person hear the information, or not?
6.challenge: Ask which of the six she would use most in a video call with a bad connection.
6.monitoring: Whether she separates hearing nothing from checking one detail.
6.evidence: Which questions she placed in another group, and her reasons.
6.transition: Move on when the six are sorted.

7.goal: To have her hear what Paula repeats in her questions, and to show the three ways to check after her answer.
run: Read the question on screen with her. Then play the meeting once, and ask her to listen for Paula's two questions.
Ask the question on screen, and let her answer before you open the button. Paula's two questions are not on screen. If she needs a question again, play the meeting and press Stop after that part.
Open Show what she does and read it with her: the card “Repeat the part you need” has Paula's two questions. Ask her to say the question with “right?” and to make the voice go up at the end.
exact: If she talks only about the days: “Why does Paula say Wednesday again? Ryan already said it.”
Practicing the intonation: “Say it with me: So the meeting is at ten, right?”
7.expected: Paula repeats “Wednesday” and “Thursday morning”, the day and the time she needs to be sure about, so Ryan and Nora can answer with a short yes. From the reveal: “Sorry, could you say that again?” — you did not hear it; “Sorry, did you say …?” — you heard it and want to check one detail; “So …, right?” — you say what you understood, and the voice goes up at the end.
7.support: If she does not remember Paula's questions, play the meeting again and press Stop after the first one. Ask about that question only, then play on to the second. If she still needs to see them, open Show what she does: the two questions are in the card “Repeat the part you need”.
7.challenge: Ask her to make one “So …, right?” question about the whole meeting.
7.monitoring: Whether she hears the rising intonation on “right?”, and whether she can produce it.
7.evidence: Her own examples, and whether the voice goes up at the end.
7.transition: Move on when the reveal has been read and she has said one question with “right?”.

8.goal: To react to short, fast updates with the right kind of question, before the longer meeting.
8.interaction: T–S, spoken, one update at a time.
run: Play the four questions one at a time, and ask her to repeat the one that is hardest to say. The words of each question stay hidden.
Open the words of a question with Show the words only if she needs to read it after two listens, and close them before the next question.
Tell her she can use the questions she heard to check your updates. Then say the updates below one at a time, at normal speed. Say one of them very fast, and in another say the number unclearly.
After each update, wait for her question. Answer it, then go to the next update.
exact: Update 1: “The client call moved to Friday at three.”
Update 2, said very fast: “The report goes out on the fifteenth.”
Update 3, with the number unclear: “We need about forty chairs for the event.”
Update 4: “The training is next week, in the big room.”
8.expected: One question after each update. Possible answers: update 1 — “Sorry, did you say Friday?” or “So the call is on Friday at three, right?”; update 2 — “Sorry, could you say that again?”; update 3 — “Sorry, did you say forty or fourteen?”; update 4 — “Just to check, is that next Monday?” Any question that checks the part she needs is correct.
8.support: If she does not ask anything, say the update again and ask: “Did you get the day?”
8.challenge: Say two updates in one sentence and let her choose what to check.
8.monitoring: Whether she chooses the right kind of question for what she did not get.
8.evidence: Which kinds of questions she used without opening the words.
8.transition: Move on when she has asked a question after each update.

9.goal: To follow a longer update in a meeting, ask when something is not clear, and confirm the main point at the end.
9.interaction: Role-play. You give the update; she is in the meeting.
run: Read the two options with her and let her choose.
With option B, ask her in one sentence what the meeting is about before you start.
Give the update below at normal speed, without stopping for her. Leave one detail unclear on purpose.
Let her ask. Answer each question briefly and continue.
At the end, wait for her to confirm what she understood. The sentence starters stay closed unless she stops.
exact: Option A, the update: “Next point: office hours. From next Monday, the office opens at eight, not at nine, and closes at five. On Fridays it closes at three. And our next management meeting is on the twenty-second, not on the fifteenth.”
Option B, the same shape: a change of day, a change of time and one number, about her situation.
If she says nothing at the end: “Any questions before we move on?”
9.expected: At least one question during the update and one confirmation at the end. For option A, a complete confirmation sounds like “So from Monday we open at eight and close at five, and at three on Fridays, right?” and a useful question is “Sorry, did you say the twenty-second?”. Option B has no fixed content: the same kinds of questions about her situation.
9.support: If she stops, point at the list on screen before you open the starters.
9.challenge: Change one detail in your answer to her question, and see if she notices.
9.monitoring: When she asks: during the update, or only at the end. Note which details she checks.
9.evidence: The questions she asked, word for word, and whether her confirmation at the end was correct.
9.transition: Move on when she has confirmed the main point.

10.goal: To keep the interaction going the other way: she gives a short update, answers two questions, asks to repeat if she needs to, and asks one question back.
10.interaction: T–S, unscripted. You are a colleague in the meeting.
run: Ask her to give a short update about the laptops or about her own work.
Ask the two questions below. Say the second one fast.
Wait after each answer. Then invite her to ask the team one question, and answer it.
exact: Question 1: “When do you need an answer from us?”
Question 2, said fast: “And who else needs to know about this before Friday?”
Handing the turn over: “Anything else you need from us?”
10.expected: A short update, then two answers. If she does not catch the second question, a complete reaction is “Sorry, could you say that again?” before she answers. If she does not know an answer, “I'm not sure. I can check and tell you.” is complete. Her question can be short, for example “Does anyone have a question?” or “Can you send me the dates by email?”.
10.support: If she answers the second question without understanding it, repeat it slowly and ask her to say it back.
10.challenge: Ask a third question with a number in it, and see if she checks it.
10.monitoring: Whether she asks for repetition when she needs it, or answers something else.
10.evidence: Whether she asked to repeat, and whether she asked a question of her own.
10.transition: Move on when she has answered two questions and asked one.

11.goal: To give one piece of feedback she can use, and to run the update again faster, with one detail changed.
11.interaction: T–S, filling the boards together, then the replay.
run: Write one thing that worked and one point to improve in the boards on screen.
Write one of her questions from screen 9 or 10 as she said it, and build a clearer version with her.

Open the replay. With option A, give the same update from screen 9 a little faster, and change one detail. With option B, ask her about the meeting she told you about, then give that update again a little faster and change one detail from what she said. She finds the change and checks it.
exact: Option A, the replay: “Next point: office hours. From next Monday, the office opens at eight and closes at six. On Fridays it closes at three. Our next management meeting is on the twenty-second.”
Option B, before the replay: “Remind me, when is that meeting? And who is going to be there?”
Option B, the replay: the same update about her meeting, a little faster, with one day, time or number different from what she told you.
11.expected: She notices that the closing time changed from five to six and checks it, for example “Sorry, did you say six? Before, it was five.” For option B, the changed detail is the one you chose; a complete reaction names it and checks it.
11.support: If she does not notice the change, ask “What time does the office close?” and let her compare.
11.challenge: Change two details instead of one.
11.monitoring: Whether the point to improve from the boards appears in the replay.
11.evidence: Whether she found the change, and whether the point to improve changed.
11.transition: Move on when the replay is done.

12.goal: To close on what was worked on, let her say how confident she feels, and leave the homework said out loud.
12.interaction: T–S, going through the recap and the confidence scale together.
run: Go through the recap list with her.
Let her fill the confidence scale herself.
Read the three lines on the right and say the homework out loud.
exact: The homework, said out loud: “This week, in a meeting or a call, check one date or number with a short question.”
12.expected: The recap has six lines: listening for the main news, listening again for details, the three kinds of questions, repeating the part you need, asking during a meeting, and answering questions about your update. The confidence scale is hers.
12.support: If she marks everything low, name one question she asked today.
12.challenge: Ask which meeting this week she could use one of the questions in.
12.monitoring: Whether her self-assessment matches what you observed.
12.evidence: Her confidence marks, and the meeting she names.
12.transition: End here. The next lesson works on connecting the ideas when she explains a problem.
